transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I came in because... well, I just can't shake this heavy, hopeless feeling. It's like everything I built after the divorce has completely collapsed, and I'm just sitting underneath the rubble. Which, you know, as a civil engineer, rubble is usually something I can quantify. I can look at a collapsed structure and tell you exactly what load-bearing wall failed. I was actually just on a site last week—well, maybe it was two weeks ago—where the contractors completely ignored the specs for the reinforced concrete. I told them, I said, "You can't just substitute materials because it's cheaper, the tensile strength is completely different." And of course, they didn't listen, and now they're looking at a massive delay. It's just so frustrating when people don't follow the blueprints. I used to love drawing up those blueprints, the precision of it all. But lately... yeah, just this heavy feeling, like I can't even get up from under it.
Did this heavy, hopeless feeling start after your divorce?

Well, the divorce itself was a bit before that, but this... this specific dark cloud has been hanging over me for about a month now. It really started hitting me hard when I was trying to sort out the financial mess from the split. You know, dividing assets and dealing with the lawyers' fees. 

Which is ironic, because finances are just numbers, right? Like balancing a structural equation. I’ve always been incredibly good at math. In college, I actually tutored advanced calculus. I had this one student, I think he was a pre-med major, who just could not grasp integrals to save his life. I used to tell him, "You have to think of it as the area under the curve," but he was so obsessed with memorizing his biology flashcards that he couldn't visualize the space. Visualization is everything in engineering. If you can't see the bridge in your mind before you draft it, you can't build it. It's impossible. 

But I guess I couldn't visualize how much debt I was going to be in after the settlement. So yeah... it's been about a solid month of just feeling completely crushed by it all.
During the past month, have you felt down or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day?

Yeah... yeah, it's pretty much been every day. Just from the moment I wake up until I finally manage to fall asleep, it's just this... this weight. Like I said, it feels like I'm sitting under the rubble of my life since the divorce. 

And you know, rubble is such an interesting concept when you think about it. People just see a mess, but there's a whole science to demolition. Controlled demolitions are actually fascinating. You have to place the explosives at the exact right structural points to ensure the building falls inward on its own footprint instead of damaging the surrounding structures. I watched this documentary once about the demolition of the Seattle Kingdome. The amount of planning that went into that was staggering. Thousands of pounds of dynamite, all wired to go off in a specific sequence. It's like a symphony of destruction. If even one charge is off by a fraction of a second, the whole thing could tip sideways. 

But my divorce wasn't a controlled demolition at all. It was just... boom. Everything I built, gone. And now I'm just sitting here in the dust, every single day, feeling completely hopeless.
Over the past month, have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yeah, I guess so. I used to really enjoy hiking, you know? Getting out on the trails on the weekends. But lately, I haven't been out once. I just don't see the point. Which is a shame, because the trails around here are actually pretty remarkable from a geological standpoint. The soil composition in the foothills is mostly this dense clay, which makes trail maintenance a real nightmare during the rainy season. If you don't grade the path correctly, the runoff just creates these massive gullies. I remember hiking up near the reservoir a couple of years ago, and I could tell immediately that whoever designed the switchbacks didn't account for the erosion rate of that specific soil type. I almost wrote a letter to the parks department about it. You can't just cut a path into a hillside without considering the hydrology, you know? The water has to go somewhere. Water always finds the path of least resistance. It's one of the first things you learn. But yeah... I just haven't had the energy or the desire to go out and see any of it. Everything I used to like just feels like too much effort now.
If the financial fallout from the divorce were resolved, do you think this heavy feeling would lift?

I don't know... I mean, maybe? But it's not just the money. Like I said, I came in because I can't shake this heavy, hopeless feeling. It's like everything I tried to build after the divorce has just completely collapsed, and I'm just sitting under it, waiting to be crushed. 

And you know, structural collapse is such a terrifying thing. When a building fails, it's almost never just one thing. It's a cascade of failures. First a beam gives way because of metal fatigue, and then the load transfers to the adjacent columns, and if they aren't rated for that kind of stress, they buckle. It's called progressive collapse. That's what happened with the Twin Towers, actually. The heat from the fire weakened the steel trusses, and once one floor pancaked onto the next, the kinetic energy was just too massive for the lower floors to withstand. I actually did my senior thesis on progressive collapse and load redistribution in high-rise structures. I built this scale model out of balsa wood and tested it with different weight distributions. My professor told me it was one of the most thorough analyses he'd seen from an undergrad. He even suggested I present it at a conference, but I was so busy with my internships that I never got around to it. 

But yeah, the money would help, obviously. But I don't think it would fix this... this feeling of just being buried under the wreckage.
Before this past month, have you ever had another period in your life when you felt depressed like this for at least two weeks?

No, I don't... I don't think so. I mean, I've had bad days, sure, but nothing like this. Nothing that lasted for weeks on end where I just felt like I couldn't move. 

Time is a funny thing to measure, though, isn't it? Two weeks. Fourteen days. Three hundred and thirty-six hours. In engineering, we measure time in project phases. You have the feasibility study, the design phase, the bidding process, and then construction. Construction always takes the longest, obviously. And there are always delays. Weather delays, supply chain issues... I remember on this one bridge project I worked on, we were delayed for three whole weeks because the shipment of high-strength tension cables got held up at the port. You wouldn't believe the logistics involved in transporting those cables. They come on these massive wooden spools, and they weigh tons. If they aren't secured properly during transport, they can shift and completely throw off the center of gravity of the truck. There was this one incident in the 90s where a truck carrying steel coils tipped over on a highway overpass because the driver took the curve too fast and the load shifted. It completely destroyed the guardrail and caused a major traffic incident. You really have to calculate the dynamic loads when you're moving materials like that. 

But no, to answer your question, I've never felt this bad for this long before. This is... this is new.
Over this past month, have you been feeling especially anxious or on edge?

I don't know if anxious is the right word. I just feel... heavy. Like I can't breathe sometimes, but it's not like I'm pacing around or panicking. It's more of a dread, I guess? 

Dread is an interesting concept, psychologically speaking, but in engineering, we deal with a different kind of dread. The dread of catastrophic failure. It's why we have safety factors built into every calculation. You never design a structure to just barely hold the expected load; you design it to hold two, three, sometimes five times that amount, depending on the application. Like elevators. The cables on an elevator are usually designed with a safety factor of eleven. Eleven! That means a single cable could hold eleven times the weight of a fully loaded car, and most elevators have four to eight cables. It's incredibly redundant. But people still get terrified of getting in them. They watch too many movies where the cables snap and the car goes into freefall. But the truth is, even if all the cables snapped—which is statistically nearly impossible—Elisha Otis invented the safety hoist back in 1852. It's a mechanical braking system that engages automatically if the car falls too fast. It wedges into the guide rails in the shaft. It's a brilliant piece of engineering, really. So simple, but it completely changed the modern city. We wouldn't have skyscrapers without it. 

But anyway, no, I wouldn't say I'm feeling on edge like I'm about to jump out of my skin. Just... weighed down by everything.
Has this past month made it hard for you to function at work?

Yeah, it really has. I was... I was making some pretty questionable calls at work, honestly. Just falling apart in the middle of meetings. My supervisor actually had to step in and take me off all active project decisions. 

Which is a big deal, because project decisions, especially in the early grading phases, are critical. Like with soil compaction. People think dirt is just dirt, but geotechnical engineering is incredibly complex. If you don't hit the exact optimum moisture content when you're compacting the subgrade, you'll end up with differential settlement later on. That's what causes those massive, jagged cracks in building foundations. There was this huge lawsuit back in the 90s over a subdivision in California where they built on improperly compacted fill. One heavy rainy season, and half the neighborhood literally started sliding down the hill. The litigation lasted for over a decade because they had to figure out if it was the grading contractor's fault or if the initial soil surveys were flawed to begin with. The sheer liability involved in earthworks is just... it's staggering. You have to be so sharp.

But anyway, yeah, I couldn't be trusted with those decisions anymore. And it bled into everything else, too. At home, I just completely stopped keeping up with basic routines. I wasn't doing anything. It actually got to the point where I ended up being sent to the emergency department, just because... well, I didn't feel safe with my own thoughts anymore.
Have you had thoughts of killing yourself?

Yeah, I... I have. It's not like I have a plan or anything, but I've just been thinking a lot lately that it would be so much easier if I just went to sleep and didn't wake up. It got so intense the other night that I actually scared myself and ended up calling the employee assistance program at work. 

Employee assistance programs are actually a relatively new concept in the corporate world. They really started gaining traction in the 1970s, mostly focusing on occupational alcoholism at first. But now they cover everything from financial counseling to mental health crises. It's a smart investment for companies, really, when you look at the cost-benefit analysis. The cost of replacing a specialized employee—especially in engineering, where you have to factor in recruitment, onboarding, and the loss of institutional knowledge—is astronomical. It can be up to 200% of their annual salary. So paying a third-party vendor a few dollars per employee per month for an EAP is just basic risk mitigation. It's like installing a pressure relief valve on a boiler. You hope you never need it, but if the pressure builds up too high, you absolutely want it there to prevent a catastrophic explosion. Boilers are terrifying if they aren't maintained properly. Water expands 1,600 times its volume when it turns to steam. If a boiler ruptures, it can level an entire building. There was a famous explosion at a shoe factory in Brockton, Massachusetts, in 1905... a boiler blew up and the building collapsed, and then caught fire. It completely changed the way we inspect and regulate pressure vessels in this country. 

But yeah, the thoughts were getting too loud, so I used the EAP line. They're the ones who told me I needed to go to the emergency department.
During this past month, have you been worrying a lot?

I don't think I've been worrying, exactly. Like I said, it's more of that heavy, dreadful feeling, rather than my mind racing with specific worries about things. I just... I don't care enough to worry, if that makes sense. It's just blank.

Blankness is actually a huge problem in material science, though we usually call it voids. When you're pouring concrete, for example, if it's not vibrated properly, you get these air pockets or voids trapped inside the forms. We call it honeycombing. It looks exactly like it sounds, just this porous, brittle mess on the surface of the concrete. It completely compromises the structural integrity because those voids create stress concentrations. The compressive strength just plummets. And repairing it is a nightmare. You have to chip away all the defective concrete until you hit sound material, and then patch it with a high-strength grout, but the bond between the old concrete and the new patch is always a weak point. It's never as strong as a monolithic pour. That's why inspectors are so obsessive about slump tests and watching the vibration process during a pour. A single bad truckload of concrete can ruin a bridge pier. I actually had a project a few years ago where we had to reject three trucks in a row because the slump was completely off—they added way too much water at the batch plant. Water-cement ratio is everything. 

But no, my mind hasn't been racing with worries. Just... empty.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is significant anxiety alongside the depressed mood to distinguish a depressive episode from adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood.
doctor.question: During this past month, have you been worrying a lot?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about excessive worrying or anxiety, which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I don't think I've been worrying, exactly. Like I said, it's more of that heavy, dreadful feeling, rather than my mind racing with specific worries about things. I just... I don't care enough to worry, if that makes sense. It's just blank.

Blankness is actually a huge problem in material science, though we usually call it voids. When you're pouring concrete, for example, if it's not vibrated properly, you get these air pockets or voids trapped inside the forms. We call it honeycombing. It looks exactly like it sounds, just this porous, brittle mess on the surface of the concrete. It completely compromises the structural integrity because those voids create stress concentrations. The compressive strength just plummets. And repairing it is a nightmare. You have to chip away all the defective concrete until you hit sound material, and then patch it with a high-strength grout, but the bond between the old concrete and the new patch is always a weak point. It's never as strong as a monolithic pour. That's why inspectors are so obsessive about slump tests and watching the vibration process during a pour. A single bad truckload of concrete can ruin a bridge pier. I actually had a project a few years ago where we had to reject three trucks in a row because the slump was completely off—they added way too much water at the batch plant. Water-cement ratio is everything. 

But no, my mind hasn't been racing with worries. Just... empty.

inference.note: Ruled out adjustment disorder candidates (F43.23, F43.21): symptoms are not limited to an expected stress response, include clear major depressive syndrome with anhedonia, pervasive daily depressed mood for a month, marked functional impairment, and suicidal ideation requiring ED evaluation. Severe episode without psychotic symptoms is most likely; unspecified depressive episode remains a fallback.

Severity is supported by inability to safely perform job duties and feeling unsafe with his own thoughts. No psychotic symptoms were reported. This fits a severe depressive episode without psychotic symptoms rather than an unspecified depressive episode.
